### Problem: Minimum Absolute Difference {#sec-srt-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `arr` of $n$ **distinct** integers ($2 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^6 \le \mathit{arr}[i] \le 10^6$). Find every pair of elements whose absolute difference equals the smallest absolute difference attained by *any* pair, and return those pairs as $[a, b]$ with $a < b$, listed in ascending order.

Source: [LC 1200 · Minimum Absolute Difference](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-absolute-difference/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Over all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs the closest two numbers are easy to miss, but sorting changes the picture: **once the array is sorted, the minimum difference is attained by some *adjacent* pair.** If $x < y < z$, then $z - x = (y - x) + (z - y)$ is at least each of the two smaller gaps, so a pair with a value between them is never strictly closer than a neighbouring pair. That collapses $O(n^2)$ pair checks into one $O(n)$ scan of $n-1$ gaps, down a sorted array. This is @sec-srt-p1's thesis: sort, then look only at neighbours.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every pair.** For each $i < j$ compute $|\mathit{arr}[i] - \mathit{arr}[j]|$, keep the smallest, and collect every pair at that distance. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space — the oracle that proves the fast form.
2. **Insertion sort, then scan neighbours.** Get sortedness the honest way — sink each element into the sorted prefix with adjacent swaps — then run the neighbour scan. Same $O(n^2)$ *time* as the brute force in the worst case (best case $O(n)$ on nearly-sorted input), but the two halves of the work are cleanly separated: sorting is the reusable tool, the scan is the pattern.
3. **Sort with the built-in, then scan neighbours.** Sort once via `sorted()` / `std::sort`; the answer gaps are all $\le$ any non-adjacent gap, so a single left-to-right pass over adjacent differences finds the minimum *and* collects the pairs realising it. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the sorted copy.

**Invariant.** After sorting into `b`, every pair's difference is at least the smallest adjacent gap, so $\text{best} = \min_i (b[i+1] - b[i])$; the required answer is exactly the adjacent pairs whose gap equals `best` (already produced in ascending order).
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every pair

::: {.form-next}
Check all $\binom{n}{2}$ unordered pairs, track the smallest gap seen, and rebuild the list whenever a strictly smaller gap appears. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — slow, but it is the definition of the answer and the thing the fast form is measured against.

**Worked example.** arr $= [4, 2, 1, 3]$. The six pairs and their gaps: $(4,2)\to2$, $(4,1)\to3$, $(4,3)\to1$, $(2,1)\to1$, $(2,3)\to1$, $(1,3)\to2$. The smallest gap is $1$, reached by $(4,3)$, $(2,1)$, and $(2,3)$. Written $[a,b]$ with $a<b$ and sorted ascending, that is $[[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]$ — exactly the required output, obtained with no idea of sorting.
:::

    assert str(final) == "[[1, 2]]"

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def min_abs_brute(arr):
    n, best = len(arr), math.inf
    res = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            d = abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            pair = [min(arr[i], arr[j]), max(arr[i], arr[j])]
            if d < best:
                best, res = d, [pair]
            elif d == best:
                res.append(pair)
    return sorted(res)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute force oracle
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;
vector<vector<int>> minAbsBrute(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size(), best = INT_MAX;
    vector<vector<int>> res;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j) {
            int d = abs(a[i] - a[j]);
            vector<int> p = {min(a[i], a[j]), max(a[i], a[j])};
            if (d < best) { best = d; res.clear(); res.push_back(p); }
            else if (d == best) res.push_back(p);
        }
    sort(res.begin(), res.end());
    return res;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `for i in range(n)` / `for j in range(i + 1, n)` enumerates each unordered pair once. `pair = [min(...), max(...)]` stores it in the required $a < b$ order. `if d < best` finds a strictly smaller gap and *restarts* the answer list `res = [pair]`; `elif d == best` appends another pair that ties the current minimum. Finally `sorted(res)` orders the pairs ascending (by first element, then second) as the problem demands. No sortedness of `arr` is used — this is the brute force that names the answer directly.

#### Insertion sort, then scan neighbours

::: {.form-next}
Take the *sorting half* of the fast form seriously: get the array into ascending order with the hand-written $O(n^2)$ insertion sort, then reuse the neighbour scan verbatim. Same worst-case $O(n^2)$ time as the brute force (but $O(n)$ on a nearly-sorted input), and the *point* is the split — the pair scan is replaced by "sort, then $n-1$ neighbour checks", and only the sortedness step still costs quadratic time. The next rung hands that step to the language's built-in sort and the whole thing collapses to $O(n\log n)$.

**Insertion sort, in plain words** (the Sorting Algorithms chapter studies it properly). Walk the array left to right. At each index, sink the new element toward the front by swapping it with its left neighbour while that neighbour is bigger. After $i$ passes, the first $i{+}1$ positions are sorted, and nothing to their right has been touched. Cost is $O(n^2)$ worst case (a reverse-sorted input), $O(n)$ best case (already sorted), $O(1)$ extra space.

**Worked example.** arr $= [4, 2, 1, 3]$. Pass 1 sinks $2$ past $4$: $[2, 4, 1, 3]$. Pass 2 sinks $1$ twice: $[1, 2, 4, 3]$. Pass 3 sinks $3$ past $4$: $[1, 2, 3, 4]$. Then one neighbour scan sees gaps $1, 1, 1$ — minimum $1$, three winning pairs.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1200-ins
def min_abs_ins(arr):
    b = list(arr)
    for i in range(1, len(b)):
        j = i
        while j > 0 and b[j - 1] > b[j]:
            b[j - 1], b[j] = b[j], b[j - 1]
            j -= 1                                  # sink b[i] into the sorted prefix
    best = min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))
    return [[b[i], b[i + 1]] for i in range(len(b) - 1) if b[i + 1] - b[i] == best]

for _ in range(300):
    arr = random.sample(range(-50, 51), random.randint(2, 12))
    assert min_abs_ins(arr) == min_abs_brute(arr)
assert min_abs_ins([4, 2, 1, 3]) == [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]
print("min_abs_ins OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> minimumAbsDifferenceIns(vector<int> b) {
    int n = (int)b.size();
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
        int j = i;
        while (j > 0 && b[j - 1] > b[j]) {
            std::swap(b[j - 1], b[j]);
            --j;
        }
    }
    int best = INT_MAX;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) best = min(best, b[i] - b[i - 1]);
    vector<vector<int>> res;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i)
        if (b[i] - b[i - 1] == best) res.push_back({b[i - 1], b[i]});
    return res;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{4, 2, 1, 3}; minimumAbsDifferenceIns(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The outer `for i in range(1, len(b))` walks the array left to right; the inner `while j > 0 and b[j-1] > b[j]` swaps the new element toward the front as long as its left neighbour is bigger. After pass $i$, positions $0..i$ are sorted — this is the picture in the board above. The two lines after the loops are already written for the optimal form; **they are the same code, character by character** — only the way we get sortedness changes. That is the ladder's whole point: the pattern is a *scan on top of a sort*, and each rung just buys the sortedness cheaper.

#### Sort with the built-in, then scan neighbours

::: {.form-next}
Hand the sortedness step to `sorted()` / `std::sort`. Now the whole thing costs $O(n\log n)$, and the neighbour scan is unchanged from form 2. This is the pattern in its purest form: sorting buys you the fact that **the answer is local** (neighbours), which no unsorted array can promise.

**Why neighbours are enough, in plain words.** In a sorted list, any two elements with stuff between them are *further* apart than at least one adjacent step. Formally, for $i < j$ the gap $b[j] - b[i] = (b[i+1]-b[i]) + \dots + (b[j]-b[j-1])$ is a sum of adjacent gaps, so it can never be smaller than the smallest single adjacent gap. Hence the minimum is some adjacent gap, and you only ever compare $b[i+1]$ with $b[i]$.

**Worked example.** arr $= [4, 2, 1, 3]$ sorted to $b = [1, 2, 3, 4]$. Adjacent gaps: $2-1=1$, $3-2=1$, $4-3=1$. Minimum $=1$, and all three adjacent pairs tie it, so the scan emits $[[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]$ — the same answer as the $O(n^2)$ pair scan and the same answer as the insertion-sort rung, in $O(n\log n)$ instead of $O(n^2)$.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1200-scan
def min_abs_scan(arr):
    b = sorted(arr)
    best = min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))
    return [[b[i], b[i + 1]] for i in range(len(b) - 1) if b[i + 1] - b[i] == best]

for _ in range(300):
    arr = random.sample(range(-50, 51), random.randint(2, 12))   # distinct
    assert min_abs_scan(arr) == min_abs_brute(arr)
assert min_abs_scan([4, 2, 1, 3]) == [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]         # LC example; the board sample
assert min_abs_scan([1, 3, 6, 10, 15]) == [[1, 3]]                     # LC example
assert min_abs_scan([3, 8, -10, 23, 19, -4, -14, 27]) == \
    [[-14, -10], [19, 23], [23, 27]]                                   # LC example
print("min_abs_scan OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> minimumAbsDifference(vector<int> a) {
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    int best = INT_MAX;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) best = min(best, a[i] - a[i - 1]);
    vector<vector<int>> res;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); ++i)
        if (a[i] - a[i - 1] == best) res.push_back({a[i - 1], a[i]});
    return res;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{4, 2, 1, 3}; minimumAbsDifference(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `b = sorted(arr)` produces the order that makes the answer local. `best = min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for ...)` is the smallest adjacent gap — by the sum argument, the global minimum gap — using the distinctness guarantee that each $b[i+1] - b[i] > 0$. The last line returns every adjacent pair whose gap equals `best`; because `b` is sorted they come out in ascending order and each pair is already $a < b$, so no post-sorting is needed. The two-pass shape (find `best`, then collect) mirrors the brute's track-then-restart, but over $n-1$ neighbours instead of $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every pair** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Insertion sort + scan** is $O(n^2)$ worst-case time / $O(n)$ best case, $O(1)$ extra space beyond the array copy — same asymptotic ceiling as the brute force, but the work is *factored* (sorting is reusable, the scan is $O(n)$). **Built-in sort + scan** is $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space (the sorted copy; $O(1)$ extra if you sort in place). Once sorted, the scan is $O(n)$ and — this is the reusable prize — every "closest pair", "smallest gap", "minimum difference" question becomes an adjacent scan, which is why @sec-srt-p1-b is the *same* code with a story change.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Distinctness is guaranteed, so no gap is $0$; if duplicates were allowed they'd answer "difference $0$" instantly.
- The pairs must be listed $a < b$ and ascending: sorting `arr` gives that for free, but the brute's `sorted(res)` is what enforces it — drop it and $[2,1]$-style pairs leak in.
- Gaps fit in $2\cdot10^6$, so plain `int` is safe here (@sec-arr-cost); do not carry that to a $10^9$ problem.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1399A · Remove Smallest](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1399/A){rating="800"} — sort, then every adjacent gap must be at most $1$.
- [LC 532 · K-diff Pairs in an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/k-diff-pairs-in-an-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — pairs at a fixed difference instead of the smallest one; sort, then two pointers or a set.
:::
